name: Hildegard of Bingen
bio: Benedictine abbess, visionary writer and composer, Hildegard wrote some of the most distinctive chant of the Middle Ages and the earliest surviving morality play with music.
bio_full: Hildegard was born in 1098 into a noble family in the Rhineland and, as a child of about eight, was placed with the anchoress Jutta at the monastery of Disibodenberg. She took vows there and in 1136 succeeded Jutta as head of the community of nuns. From her early forties she recorded the visions she had experienced since childhood, beginning with Scivias, and with papal approval became famous across Europe. Around 1150 she founded her own convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen, and later a second across the Rhine at Eibingen. She corresponded with popes, emperors and Bernard of Clairvaux, wrote on medicine and natural history, and undertook preaching tours, which was extraordinary for a woman of her time. She died in 1179 and was formally canonised and named a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

About seventy of Hildegard's chants survive, gathered under the title Symphonia armonie celestium revelationum, together with the sung drama Ordo Virtutum. Her melodies sound unlike most plainchant: they leap widely, span unusually large ranges and spin long, ecstatic phrases out of a few recurring motifs, setting her own vivid Latin poetry rich in images of greenness, light and the Virgin. She thought of music as an echo of the harmony of heaven lost at the Fall. Largely forgotten for centuries, her music was rediscovered in the late twentieth century through recordings, and she is now among the best-known composers of the Middle Ages.

name: Léonin
bio: The first named composer of polyphony, Léonin is credited with the Magnus liber organi, the great book of two-voice organum for the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris.
bio_full: Almost all we know about Léonin comes from an English student in Paris in the late thirteenth century, known as Anonymous IV, who called him the best composer of organum and said he made the Magnus liber organi for the services of Notre-Dame. Scholars have identified him, with some probability, with a Leonius who was a canon of Notre-Dame and a poet, active from the 1150s until about 1201. He would thus have worked while the new Gothic cathedral was being built, a setting that mirrors the new soaring music.

Léonin's organum takes a chant and slows it down so that each note is held as a long drone, while a second voice sings flowing, melismatic lines above. In other sections, called discant, both voices move in measured rhythm. The Magnus liber covered the main feasts of the church year and was revised and extended by later musicians, Pérotin above all, so it survives only in later, altered copies. The idea that a composer might be named and remembered, and the system of rhythmic modes the book helped establish, mark the beginning of the written polyphonic tradition of Western music.

name: Pérotin
bio: Pérotin revised Léonin's Magnus liber and composed monumental organum for three and four voices, among the earliest music of such scale in Europe.
bio_full: Pérotin, called Perotinus Magnus by Anonymous IV, worked at Notre-Dame in Paris around 1200. Little is certain about his life; some scholars have linked him with a cathedral official called Petrus, but this is debated. Anonymous IV credits him with improving Léonin's Magnus liber organi by writing shorter discant sections, called clausulae, and with composing organum for four voices, including Viderunt omnes and Sederunt principes. Edicts issued by the Bishop of Paris in 1198 and 1199 calling for such organa at Christmas and on St Stephen's Day help date this music.

Pérotin's four-voice organa build huge blocks of sound above sustained chant notes, with the upper voices locked in bright, dancing rhythmic patterns that interlock and exchange phrases. The effect is hypnotic, and twentieth-century listeners have compared it with minimalism; Steve Reich among others admired it. His clausulae, once words were added to their upper voices, became one of the sources of the motet, the main genre of the thirteenth century. With Léonin he stands at the head of the history of Western composition.

name: Guillaume de Machaut
bio: Poet and composer, Machaut was the dominant figure of the French Ars nova, and his Messe de Nostre Dame is the earliest complete setting of the Mass by a single known composer.
bio_full: Machaut was born around 1300, probably in Champagne, and was educated as a cleric. From about 1323 he served as secretary to John of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia, travelling with him across Europe until John's death at the battle of Crécy in 1346. He was rewarded with a canonry at Reims Cathedral, where he spent much of the rest of his life, while also serving as poet and musician to members of the French royal family and the high nobility. In his later years he supervised lavish manuscript collections of his complete works, an unusual concern with his own legacy. He died in Reims in 1377.

Machaut was as famous a poet as a composer, and his long narrative poems influenced Chaucer. His music includes motets, often isorhythmic, built on repeating patterns of rhythm and pitch, and more than a hundred songs in the courtly fixed forms of ballade, rondeau and virelai, with refined, supple melodies over two or three lower parts. His rondeau Ma fin est mon commencement can be sung forwards and backwards. The Messe de Nostre Dame, probably for the cathedral at Reims, gives the mass a unity unknown before. Because his works were collected so carefully, they survive more fully than those of any other medieval composer.

name: Guillaume Du Fay
bio: The leading composer of the early fifteenth century, Du Fay wrote masses, motets and chansons that set the course for Renaissance polyphony.
bio_full: Du Fay was probably born around 1397 near Brussels and grew up as a choirboy at Cambrai Cathedral. In the 1420s he worked in Italy for the Malatesta family and then in the papal chapel, and he spent long periods at the court of Savoy. In 1436 he wrote the motet Nuper rosarum flores for the consecration of Florence Cathedral beneath Brunelleschi's new dome. From 1439 he was based mainly at Cambrai, where he was a canon and a respected figure until his death in 1474, keeping close ties with Italy, Savoy and the Burgundian court.

Du Fay's career spans the change from late medieval to Renaissance music. His early motets still use isorhythm, but he absorbed the warm, full harmony of English composers such as Dunstable and the smooth melodies of Italy. He helped develop the cyclic mass, in which all movements share a borrowed tune, writing masses on the song L'homme armé and on his own chanson Se la face ay pale. His chansons and hymns are melodious and clear in texture. Contemporaries ranked him the foremost composer of his age, and his works shaped the generation of Ockeghem and Josquin.

name: Josquin des Prez
bio: Hailed in his lifetime as the greatest composer of his age, Josquin combined expressive word-setting with mastery of imitative counterpoint in masses, motets and chansons.
bio_full: Josquin des Prez was born around 1450, probably in the French-speaking region of Hainaut or Picardy. Documents once thought to trace his early career turned out to belong to another singer, and his biography has been heavily revised by modern research. He served the Sforza family in Milan in the 1480s, sang in the papal chapel in Rome around 1489–94, and in 1503–04 was maestro di cappella to Duke Ercole d'Este in Ferrara, where he wrote the Missa Hercules Dux Ferrariae. He spent his last years as provost of the collegiate church at Condé-sur-l'Escaut, where he died in 1521.

Josquin's music unites technical brilliance with a new attention to the meaning and sound of words. He used pervading imitation, in which all voices take up the same motif in turn, and he paired voices in clear, sonorous dialogue, as in the motet Ave Maria ... virgo serena. His masses range from strict canon to the paraphrase of a chant throughout every voice, as in the Missa Pange lingua. Ottaviano Petrucci, the first printer of polyphonic music, devoted three books to his masses, and Martin Luther said Josquin was master of the notes, which must do as he wished. Some works once credited to him are now judged doubtful, a lively area of scholarly debate.

name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
bio: Palestrina's serene, balanced polyphony for the Catholic church became the model of Renaissance sacred style, studied by composers for centuries.
bio_full: Giovanni Pierluigi took his name from the town of Palestrina near Rome, where he was born around 1525. He was organist and choirmaster at the cathedral there before Pope Julius III, formerly bishop of Palestrina, brought him to Rome in 1551. He held posts at the Cappella Giulia of St Peter's, St John Lateran and Santa Maria Maggiore, sang briefly in the Sistine Chapel choir, and from 1571 until his death directed the Cappella Giulia again. He lost his first wife and two sons to plague, and later married a wealthy widow, whose fur business helped fund the printing of his works. He died in Rome in 1594.

Palestrina wrote more than a hundred masses, several hundred motets, hymns, Magnificats and madrigals. His style is a model of controlled flowing lines, careful treatment of dissonance and transparent texture, so that the words remain audible. A legend that his Missa Papae Marcelli persuaded the Council of Trent not to ban polyphony is now regarded as a myth, but it shows his reputation as the saviour of church music. Johann Joseph Fux's 1725 treatise Gradus ad Parnassum codified a version of his style, and generations of students, including Haydn and Mozart, learned counterpoint from it.

name: Thomas Tallis
bio: Tallis served four Tudor monarchs through the upheavals of the English Reformation and wrote the forty-voice motet Spem in alium.
bio_full: Thomas Tallis was born around 1505 and worked at Dover Priory, in London and at Waltham Abbey until its dissolution in 1540. He then sang at Canterbury Cathedral before joining the Chapel Royal around 1543, where he served under Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary I and Elizabeth I, adapting his music to each change in the official religion. In 1575 Elizabeth granted him and his younger colleague William Byrd a monopoly on printing music and music paper, and they published the Cantiones sacrae that year. He died in Greenwich in 1585.

Tallis's music moves from the florid Latin antiphons of the pre-Reformation church to the plain, syllabic English anthems required under Edward VI, such as If ye love me, and back to elaborate Latin works under Mary. His two settings of the Lamentations of Jeremiah are deeply expressive, and his tunes for Archbishop Parker's psalter include the melody Ralph Vaughan Williams used in his Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis. Spem in alium, for forty independent voices, is among the most ambitious works of the Renaissance.

name: William Byrd
bio: The greatest English composer of his age, Byrd was a Catholic in Protestant England who wrote for the Anglican church, for secret Catholic worship and for the keyboard.
bio_full: Byrd was born around 1540 in London and probably studied with Tallis. In 1563 he became organist of Lincoln Cathedral, and in 1572 he joined the Chapel Royal, sharing its organist's post with Tallis. Although he and his family were recusants, repeatedly fined for refusing Anglican services, he kept the favour of Elizabeth I. In the 1590s he moved to Stondon Massey in Essex, near the Catholic household of Sir John Petre, and wrote music for the clandestine masses held there. He died in 1623.

Byrd's output covers almost every genre of his time. His three masses, for three, four and five voices, were printed discreetly without title pages in the 1590s, and his two books of Gradualia provided music for the Catholic church year. For the Anglican rite he wrote the Great Service and many anthems. His keyboard music, collected in My Ladye Nevells Booke and the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book, laid the foundations of an English keyboard school, and his consort songs and music for viols are equally distinguished.

name: Orlande de Lassus
bio: One of the most prolific and versatile composers of the Renaissance, Lassus wrote more than two thousand works in Latin, French, Italian and German.
bio_full: Orlande de Lassus, also known as Orlando di Lasso, was born around 1532 in Mons. According to a story that may be legend, his beautiful voice led to his being kidnapped three times as a boy. He spent his youth in Italy, in the service of the Gonzaga and in Naples and Rome, where he briefly directed the choir of St John Lateran. After time in Antwerp he joined the court of Duke Albrecht V of Bavaria in Munich in 1556, leading its chapel from the 1560s until his death in 1594. He travelled widely and was ennobled by Emperor Maximilian II.

Lassus mastered every genre of his age: masses, motets, Magnificats, Italian madrigals and villanellas, French chansons and German lieder. His style is vivid and dramatic, quick to paint the words in sound, by turns earthy and humorous or intensely penitential, as in the Penitential Psalms and his final cycle, the Lagrime di San Pietro. With Palestrina he represents the summit of late Renaissance polyphony, and his works were printed and reprinted across Europe.

name: Giovanni Gabrieli
bio: Organist at St Mark's in Venice, Gabrieli wrote splendid works for divided choirs and brass that bridged the Renaissance and the Baroque.
bio_full: Giovanni Gabrieli was born in Venice in the mid-1550s and studied with his uncle Andrea Gabrieli, organist at St Mark's. He spent several years in Munich with Lassus, then returned to Venice, becoming organist at St Mark's in 1585 and also at the Scuola Grande di San Rocco. In 1587 he published a collection of his uncle's music together with his own. His fame drew pupils from northern Europe, above all the German Heinrich Schütz. He died in Venice in 1612.

Gabrieli exploited the galleries of St Mark's, placing choirs of voices and instruments in different parts of the basilica for echoes and dialogues, a technique called cori spezzati. His Sacrae symphoniae of 1597 includes the Sonata pian' e forte, among the first pieces to specify both instruments and dynamics. His later works use contrasts of solo and tutti that point towards the Baroque concerto. Through Schütz his style passed into German Protestant music.

name: Claudio Monteverdi
bio: Monteverdi carried music from the Renaissance madrigal into the Baroque, and his Orfeo of 1607 is the earliest opera still regularly staged.
bio_full: Claudio Monteverdi was born in Cremona in 1567, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with the cathedral choirmaster Marc'Antonio Ingegneri, publishing his first music at fifteen. Around 1590 he joined the court of the Gonzaga in Mantua, becoming its maestro di cappella in 1601. There he wrote L'Orfeo (1607), and in 1610 he published the Vespers of the Blessed Virgin. In 1613 he became maestro di cappella at St Mark's in Venice, the most prestigious church post in Italy, which he held for thirty years. He took holy orders after his wife's death and in old age wrote operas for Venice's new public opera houses, including L'incoronazione di Poppea. He died in Venice in 1643.

Monteverdi published nine books of madrigals that trace the shift from the old style to the new. When the theorist Giovanni Artusi attacked his harsh dissonances, Monteverdi replied that in his second practice the words should be mistress of the music, not its servant. He embraced the basso continuo, the expressive solo voice and the concerted style with instruments, and invented an 'agitated' style (stile concitato) of rapid repeated notes for battle and anger. His operas show a deep understanding of human character, and since their twentieth-century revival they have been central to the opera repertory.

name: Jean-Baptiste Lully
bio: Florentine-born, Lully became Louis XIV's music master and created French opera, the tragédie en musique.
bio_full: Giovanni Battista Lulli was born in Florence in 1632, the son of a miller, and was taken to France at thirteen as an Italian tutor for a royal cousin. A gifted dancer and violinist, he caught the young Louis XIV's eye, danced alongside him in court ballets and in 1653 was made royal composer of instrumental music. He collaborated with Molière on comedy-ballets such as Le bourgeois gentilhomme, became a naturalised Frenchman, and in 1672 acquired a royal monopoly over opera in France. He died in 1687 from gangrene after striking his foot with the long staff he used to beat time.

With the librettist Philippe Quinault, Lully created the tragédie en musique, a five-act opera with prologue in praise of the king, closely fitted to French verse, with dances, choruses and spectacular machinery. Works such as Atys and Armide fixed this form for a century. He drilled the king's string orchestra into famous discipline and established the French overture, a slow dotted opening followed by a fast fugal section, imitated by Bach, Handel and many others.

name: Henry Purcell
bio: The finest English composer of the Baroque, Purcell wrote the opera Dido and Aeneas and a wealth of theatre, church and ceremonial music before his early death.
bio_full: Henry Purcell was born in Westminster in 1659 into a family of court musicians and sang as a boy in the Chapel Royal. In 1677 he succeeded Matthew Locke as composer for the King's violins, and in 1679 he became organist of Westminster Abbey, adding a post at the Chapel Royal in 1682. He wrote odes and anthems for the courts of Charles II, James II and William and Mary, including music for Mary's funeral in 1695. In his last years he wrote extensively for the London stage. He died in November 1695, aged only thirty-six, and is buried in Westminster Abbey near the organ.

Purcell had a special gift for setting English words, catching their rhythm and colour, and often built expressive arias over a repeating ground bass, as in Dido's lament. Besides Dido and Aeneas he wrote semi-operas such as King Arthur and The Fairy-Queen, which mix spoken drama with masques, as well as anthems, songs, trio sonatas and fantasias for viols. For two centuries after him no English-born composer matched his reputation, and Britten and Tippett championed his music in the twentieth century.

name: Arcangelo Corelli
bio: Violinist and composer, Corelli published only six collections, but they fixed the forms of the sonata and the concerto grosso for the whole Baroque.
bio_full: Arcangelo Corelli was born in 1653 at Fusignano near Ravenna and trained in Bologna, a centre of violin playing. By 1675 he was in Rome, where he spent the rest of his life under the patronage of Queen Christina of Sweden, Cardinal Benedetto Pamphili and above all Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni, in whose palace he lived. He led the orchestras for great Roman occasions and was admired as Europe's leading violinist and teacher. He died in Rome in 1713 and was buried in the Pantheon.

Corelli published four collections of trio sonatas, a book of violin sonatas (Op. 5, 1700) and the twelve Concerti grossi, Op. 6, issued after his death. His music is notable for its clarity, balance and polish, and for using chains of suspensions and strongly directed harmony that helped establish tonal major and minor keys. Reprinted constantly, his works became models for Handel, Bach, Vivaldi and generations of violinists.

name: Antonio Vivaldi
bio: The 'Red Priest' of Venice wrote hundreds of concertos, including The Four Seasons, which shaped the Baroque concerto across Europe.
bio_full: Antonio Vivaldi was born in Venice in 1678, the son of a violinist at St Mark's. He was ordained a priest in 1703, and his red hair earned him the nickname il prete rosso, but ill health, probably asthma, soon excused him from saying mass. The same year he became violin master at the Ospedale della Pietà, a Venetian home for foundling girls famous for its female orchestra and choir, with which he was associated on and off for most of his career. He also wrote and produced dozens of operas. His printed concertos, beginning with L'estro armonico in 1711, made him famous across Europe. He died poor in Vienna in 1741, having gone there probably in search of imperial patronage.

Vivaldi wrote about five hundred concertos, many for violin but also for bassoon, cello, flute, mandolin and other instruments. He established the three-movement fast-slow-fast pattern and ritornello form, in which a returning orchestral refrain alternates with solo episodes, and gave the soloist brilliant, idiomatic music. Bach transcribed several of his concertos for keyboard. Vivaldi was largely forgotten after his death, and much of his music was rediscovered only in the twentieth century, when manuscripts were found in Turin; The Four Seasons became one of the most recorded works of all.

name: Johann Sebastian Bach
bio: Bach brought Baroque counterpoint to its summit in church cantatas, Passions, keyboard and instrumental works, and is widely regarded as one of the greatest composers of all.
bio_full: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach in 1685 into a large family of musicians. Orphaned at ten, he was raised by his elder brother in Ohrdruf. After early posts as organist in Arnstadt and Mühlhausen, he served at the court of Weimar (1708–17), where he wrote much of his organ music, and then as Kapellmeister to Prince Leopold of Anhalt-Köthen (1717–23), the period of the Brandenburg Concertos and much chamber music. In 1723 he became Thomaskantor in Leipzig, responsible for the music of the city's main churches, and for some years he wrote a new cantata nearly every week. He had twenty children with two wives, several of whom became important composers. He died in Leipzig in 1750.

Bach mastered every genre of his time except opera and combined the counterpoint of the German tradition with Italian concerto form and French dance styles. His music is often of great intellectual complexity, as in the fugues of The Well-Tempered Clavier and The Art of Fugue, yet also deeply expressive, especially in the Passions and cantatas, which he wrote as acts of Lutheran devotion. In his lifetime he was best known as an organist and his style was thought old-fashioned. Mozart and Beethoven studied his music, and Mendelssohn's 1829 performance of the St Matthew Passion launched a revival that made him a foundation of the Western canon.

name: George Frideric Handel
bio: German-born and London-based, Handel was the leading composer of Italian opera in England and created the English oratorio, above all Messiah.
bio_full: Georg Friedrich Händel was born in Halle in 1685, the same year as Bach. His father wanted him to study law, but he became a violinist and harpsichordist at the Hamburg opera, and from 1706 spent four years in Italy, where he met Corelli and Scarlatti and had operas and oratorios performed with success. After a brief post as Kapellmeister to the Elector of Hanover, he settled in London, where his opera Rinaldo triumphed in 1711. When the Elector became George I of Britain, Handel remained in favour, writing the Water Music and later the coronation anthems, including Zadok the Priest. He ran opera companies for two decades and, when the fashion for Italian opera faded in the 1730s, turned to English oratorio. He became a British subject in 1727, went blind in his last years and was buried in Westminster Abbey in 1759.

Handel combined German counterpoint, Italian melody and English choral tradition. His operas, such as Giulio Cesare, are full of brilliant and moving arias, and his oratorios, from Saul and Israel in Egypt to Messiah and Jephtha, use the chorus with unprecedented grandeur. Unlike Bach, he never fell out of fashion: Messiah has been performed every year since his death, and the 1784 Handel commemoration in Westminster Abbey began the tradition of mass choral festivals. Haydn and Beethoven revered him.

name: Jean-Philippe Rameau
bio: Theorist and composer, Rameau wrote a landmark treatise on harmony and in his fifties became the leading composer of French opera.
bio_full: Jean-Philippe Rameau was born in Dijon in 1683, the son of an organist, and spent many years as an organist in provincial cathedrals. His Traité de l'harmonie, published in Paris in 1722, made his name as a theorist. He settled in Paris, published harpsichord music, and only at fifty, in 1733, produced his first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie. Its novelty divided audiences between his supporters and the followers of Lully. Over the next three decades he wrote some thirty stage works, including Les Indes galantes and Castor et Pollux, and became court composer to Louis XV. He died in Paris in 1764.

Rameau's Traité argued that harmony rests on a fundamental bass and on chords built from the natural resonance of sound, ideas that underpin the teaching of harmony to this day. His operas are richer in harmony and orchestral colour than Lully's, with vivid descriptive passages and inventive dances. In the Querelle des Bouffons of the 1750s, Rousseau and other philosophes attacked French opera in favour of Italian comic opera, making Rameau the figurehead of the old style. Debussy later hailed him as a model of French clarity.

name: Christoph Willibald Gluck
bio: Gluck reformed opera, stripping away showy display in favour of dramatic truth, as in Orfeo ed Euridice.
bio_full: Christoph Willibald Gluck was born in 1714 in Erasbach in the Upper Palatinate, the son of a forester, and grew up in Bohemia. He studied in Prague and Milan and for two decades wrote Italian operas for cities across Europe, including London. He settled in Vienna, becoming Kapellmeister of the court theatre. There, with the librettist Ranieri de' Calzabigi and the choreographer Gasparo Angiolini, he produced Orfeo ed Euridice (1762) and Alceste (1767). From 1774 he worked in Paris under the patronage of his former pupil Marie Antoinette, where his operas, including Iphigénie en Tauride, sparked a public rivalry with Niccolò Piccinni. He died in Vienna in 1787.

In the preface to Alceste Gluck explained his aim of making music serve the poetry and drama, without the singers' vanity or needless ornament. His reform operas use simpler plots, continuous orchestral accompaniment of recitative, dramatic choruses and dance, and overtures that prepare the mood of the drama. Berlioz worshipped him, and his ideas influenced Mozart and, through Berlioz and Wagner, the later history of opera.

name: Joseph Haydn
bio: Called the father of the symphony and the string quartet, Haydn spent three decades at the Esterházy court and became the most celebrated composer in Europe.
bio_full: Franz Joseph Haydn was born in 1732 in the village of Rohrau, the son of a wheelwright. He sang as a choirboy at St Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna until his voice broke, then scraped a living as a teacher and freelance musician, learning composition largely on his own. In 1761 he entered the service of the Esterházy princes, and from 1766 to 1790 he was their Kapellmeister, mostly at the remote palace of Eszterháza, writing symphonies, operas, baryton trios and church music. As he said, isolation forced him to become original. His fame spread through publication, and after Prince Nikolaus died in 1790 he made two triumphant visits to London, writing his last twelve symphonies for the impresario Johann Peter Salomon. Back in Vienna he composed The Creation and The Seasons. He died in 1809, as Napoleon's armies occupied the city.

Haydn wrote over a hundred symphonies, sixty-eight string quartets, many piano sonatas and trios, operas and masses. He did more than anyone to shape sonata form and the genres of the Classical style, developing whole movements from small motifs and treating the four players of the quartet as equal partners in conversation. His music is full of wit and surprise, but also of searching seriousness. He was a friend of Mozart, who dedicated six quartets to him, and briefly a teacher of Beethoven.

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
bio: A child prodigy who became one of the greatest of all composers, Mozart excelled in every genre of his day, from opera and the piano concerto to the symphony and chamber music.
bio_full: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the son of Leopold Mozart, a violinist and composer in the service of the Prince-Archbishop. With his sister Nannerl he was taken on long tours as a child prodigy, performing before the courts of Vienna, Paris and London, and in Italy he wrote operas for Milan while still in his teens. Back in Salzburg he chafed under Archbishop Colloredo, and in 1781 he broke with him and settled in Vienna as a freelance pianist, teacher and composer. He married Constanze Weber in 1782. The 1780s brought his great piano concertos and, with the librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte, The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and Così fan tutte. In 1791 he wrote The Magic Flute for a suburban theatre and began a Requiem, which he left unfinished when he died in December that year, aged thirty-five. Rumours that he was poisoned, by Salieri or anyone else, have no basis.

Mozart wrote more than six hundred works. His music combines melodic grace and perfect proportion with emotional depth and, in the operas, an unrivalled insight into character, so that several people can sing at once and each remain themselves. He raised the piano concerto into a dramatic dialogue and in his last symphonies and quartets reached a new complexity, including Bach-inspired counterpoint. Haydn told Leopold that his son was the greatest composer he knew. Mozart's work became a touchstone of the Classical style.

name: Ludwig van Beethoven
bio: Beethoven expanded the forms of the Classical style with unprecedented power and personal expression, and continued to compose after he became deaf.
bio_full: Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, the grandson and son of court musicians. His father, an alcoholic tenor, pushed him to perform as a prodigy, and by his teens he was playing in the court orchestra and supporting his family. In 1792 he moved to Vienna to study with Haydn and soon made his name as a fiery virtuoso pianist and improviser, supported by aristocratic patrons. Around 1798 he noticed his hearing failing; in the Heiligenstadt Testament of 1802 he wrote of his despair and resolve to go on. The following years produced the Eroica Symphony, the opera Fidelio, the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies and the Emperor Concerto. By 1818 he was totally deaf and communicated through conversation books. His last decade brought the late piano sonatas, the Missa solemnis, the Ninth Symphony and the late string quartets. He died in Vienna in 1827, and tens of thousands attended his funeral.

Beethoven inherited the forms of Haydn and Mozart and pushed them to new extremes of scale, contrast and dramatic struggle, often building whole works from tiny motifs and directing them towards a triumphant conclusion. His late works explored fugue, variation and unusual structures with a depth and strangeness that puzzled contemporaries. He saw himself as an independent artist rather than a servant of patrons, an image that shaped the Romantic idea of the composer as heroic genius. For the next century every composer of symphonies worked in his shadow.

name: Franz Schubert
bio: In a life of only thirty-one years Schubert wrote more than six hundred songs, raising the German lied to high art, as well as symphonies, chamber music and piano works of great beauty.
bio_full: Franz Schubert was born in 1797 in a suburb of Vienna, the son of a schoolmaster. He sang in the imperial court chapel choir and studied at the city's seminary, where Antonio Salieri taught him composition. He worked for a time as a teacher in his father's school but from about 1818 lived precariously as a composer, supported by a circle of devoted friends who held musical evenings, the Schubertiades, devoted to his music. Only a small part of his output was published or performed publicly in his lifetime. In late 1822 he contracted syphilis, and he died in 1828, possibly of typhoid, a year after Beethoven, beside whom he was later reburied.

Schubert's songs, including Erlkönig, Gretchen am Spinnrade and the cycles Die schöne Müllerin and Winterreise, give the piano a role equal to the voice, painting scenes and states of mind. His instrumental music, such as the Unfinished Symphony, the Great C major Symphony, the String Quintet and the last piano sonatas, combines Classical forms with expansive lyricism and bold harmonic shifts. Much of it was discovered after his death: Schumann found the Great C major Symphony and Mendelssohn conducted its premiere in 1839.

name: Gioachino Rossini
bio: The most popular opera composer of his day, Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville and some forty operas before retiring from the stage at thirty-seven.
bio_full: Gioachino Rossini was born in Pesaro in 1792 to musician parents and studied in Bologna. His first opera was staged in Venice in 1810, and within a few years he was the leading composer in Italy, writing up to four operas a year. Tancredi and L'italiana in Algeri (both 1813) and Il barbiere di Siviglia (1816) made him famous across Europe, and he spent several years writing for Naples. In 1824 he moved to Paris, where his last opera, Guillaume Tell, appeared in 1829. He then wrote no more operas, for reasons of health and perhaps changing taste, though he later wrote a Stabat Mater, the Petite messe solennelle and many piano and vocal pieces. He died near Paris in 1868.

Rossini's comic operas are celebrated for their sparkle and energy, especially the famous Rossini crescendo, in which a phrase repeats with ever-growing orchestration. His serious operas developed the conventions of Italian romantic opera that Bellini, Donizetti and the young Verdi inherited. Guillaume Tell helped create French grand opera. His wit and gastronomy became legendary, and Barber has never left the repertoire.

name: Hector Berlioz
bio: A pioneer of the Romantic programme symphony and of modern orchestration, Berlioz wrote the Symphonie fantastique and the epic opera Les Troyens.
bio_full: Hector Berlioz was born in 1803 in La Côte-Saint-André near Grenoble, the son of a doctor, and was sent to Paris to study medicine. Overwhelmed by the opera, he switched to music and entered the Conservatoire, eventually winning the Prix de Rome in 1830. That year the Symphonie fantastique, inspired by his obsession with the Irish actress Harriet Smithson, whom he later married, announced his radical originality. He wrote music criticism to make a living, conducted his works across Europe, especially in Germany and Russia, and published a treatise on orchestration. His opera Les Troyens was never staged complete in his lifetime. He died in Paris in 1869.

Berlioz drew inspiration from literature, from Shakespeare, Byron, Goethe and Virgil, and often gave his works explicit narratives, as in Harold en Italie and Roméo et Juliette. He thought in terms of orchestral colour, used huge forces when he wanted them, as in the Grande messe des morts, and also wrote music of great delicacy. His Grand traité d'instrumentation became a standard text, and his ideas influenced Liszt, Wagner and Russian composers. His reputation in France grew slowly, and his full stature was recognised only in the twentieth century.

name: Felix Mendelssohn
bio: Composer, pianist and conductor, Mendelssohn wrote polished Romantic works such as A Midsummer Night's Dream and led the revival of Bach.
bio_full: Jakob Ludwig Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy was born in Hamburg in 1809, the grandson of the philosopher Moses Mendelssohn, into a wealthy family that had converted from Judaism to Lutheranism. A prodigy comparable to Mozart, he wrote the String Octet at sixteen and the overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream at seventeen. In 1829 he conducted the St Matthew Passion in Berlin, its first performance since Bach's death. He travelled widely, especially in Britain, where he was a favourite of Queen Victoria and premiered Elijah in Birmingham in 1846. As conductor of the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra from 1835, he built one of Europe's finest orchestras, and in 1843 he founded the Leipzig Conservatory. Exhausted by overwork and grief over the death of his sister Fanny, herself a gifted composer, he died in 1847 at thirty-eight.

Mendelssohn combined Romantic imagination with Classical poise and craftsmanship. His Hebrides overture and Scottish and Italian symphonies evoke landscape, his Violin Concerto in E minor remains one of the most loved, and his Songs without Words were played in homes everywhere. He did much to create the modern concert repertoire of past masterpieces. After his death his reputation suffered, partly from antisemitic attacks, most notoriously Wagner's essay of 1850, and the Nazis banned his music.

name: Frédéric Chopin
bio: Chopin wrote almost exclusively for the piano, creating a deeply personal poetry of the instrument in nocturnes, études, ballades, mazurkas and polonaises.
bio_full: Fryderyk Chopin was born in 1810 at Żelazowa Wola near Warsaw, to a French father and Polish mother, and grew up in Warsaw, where he studied at the conservatory and was celebrated as a prodigy. He left Poland in 1830, shortly before the November Uprising against Russian rule, and never returned. Settling in Paris in 1831, he preferred playing in aristocratic salons to large concert halls and earned his living mainly by teaching and publishing. From 1838 to 1847 he had a relationship with the novelist George Sand, spending summers at her house at Nohant, where he wrote much of his finest music. Suffering from tuberculosis, he gave his last concerts in Britain in 1848 and died in Paris in 1849.

Chopin transformed the piano's possibilities with singing melodies inspired by Italian opera, rich chromatic harmony, subtle use of the pedal and flexible rubato. His études turn technical exercises into concert music; his ballades and scherzos are large dramatic forms; his mazurkas and polonaises draw on Polish dance and became symbols of national feeling. Schumann greeted him in print with the words, 'Hats off, gentlemen, a genius!' His music remains central to every pianist's repertoire.

name: Robert Schumann
bio: Schumann's piano cycles, songs and symphonies embody literary Romanticism, and as a critic he championed Chopin and Brahms.
bio_full: Robert Schumann was born in Zwickau in 1810, the son of a bookseller and publisher, and grew up steeped in literature. He studied law but turned to music, training as a pianist with Friedrich Wieck in Leipzig until an injury to his right hand ended his hopes of a concert career. In 1834 he founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, writing as the impetuous Florestan and the dreamy Eusebius. After a long legal battle with Wieck he married Wieck's daughter Clara in 1840, the year he wrote some 140 songs. He worked in Leipzig, Dresden and from 1850 as music director in Düsseldorf. He suffered from severe depression; in 1854 he threw himself into the Rhine and was committed at his own request to an asylum at Endenich, where he died in 1856.

Schumann's piano music, including Carnaval, Kinderszenen and Kreisleriana, consists of cycles of short, characterful pieces full of hidden references, codes and literary allusions. His songs, such as Dichterliebe, give the piano a poetic voice of its own. He also wrote four symphonies, a Piano Concerto and chamber music. In his last essay, New Paths, he hailed the young Brahms. His blend of intimacy and fantasy is the essence of German Romanticism.

name: Clara Schumann
bio: One of the great pianists of the nineteenth century, Clara Schumann was also a gifted composer and the leading interpreter of her husband's and Brahms's music.
bio_full: Clara Wieck was born in Leipzig in 1819 and trained by her father, Friedrich Wieck, as a piano prodigy. She toured Europe from childhood, winning the admiration of Goethe, Paganini and Liszt, and was named a royal and imperial chamber virtuoso in Vienna at eighteen. In 1840 she married Robert Schumann against her father's opposition. She bore eight children, managed the household and kept performing, and after Robert's breakdown and death she supported the family through concert tours across Europe, including many visits to Britain. She was a close friend of Johannes Brahms for over forty years. From 1878 she taught at the Hoch Conservatory in Frankfurt, where she died in 1896.

Clara Schumann composed mostly before 1854, including a Piano Concerto begun at fourteen, a Piano Trio in G minor, songs and piano pieces such as the Variations on a Theme by Robert Schumann. She doubted herself as a composer, once writing that a woman must not desire to compose. As a performer she helped change concert life, playing from memory and favouring serious works by Beethoven, Chopin, Robert Schumann and Brahms over showpieces. Her music has been revived and recorded widely since the 1970s.

name: Franz Liszt
bio: The supreme piano virtuoso of the nineteenth century, Liszt also invented the symphonic poem and pointed the way to modern harmony.
bio_full: Franz Liszt was born in 1811 at Raiding, in the Hungarian part of the Habsburg empire, where his father worked for the Esterházy family. He studied in Vienna with Czerny and Salieri, then moved to Paris, where Paganini's virtuosity inspired him to transform piano technique. Between 1839 and 1847 he toured Europe from Lisbon to Moscow, provoking the frenzy that Heinrich Heine called Lisztomania. He then settled in Weimar as court music director, championing new music including Wagner's Lohengrin, and writing his symphonic poems. Thwarted in his plan to marry Princess Carolyne zu Sayn-Wittgenstein, he moved to Rome and took minor orders in the church in 1865. In later life he divided his time between Rome, Weimar and Budapest, teaching without fee. He died in Bayreuth in 1886, where his daughter Cosima was Wagner's widow.

Liszt's piano works, from the Transcendental Études and Hungarian Rhapsodies to the Sonata in B minor, demanded new technique and helped create the modern piano recital. His symphonic poems, such as Les préludes, were orchestral works inspired by poetry or painting and built through the transformation of themes. His late pieces, spare and harmonically daring, anticipate Debussy, Bartók and even atonality. A generous teacher and promoter of other composers, he was a central figure of the New German School.

name: Richard Wagner
bio: Wagner remade opera as music drama, writing his own librettos and creating the Ring cycle, Tristan und Isolde and a theatre at Bayreuth for his works.
bio_full: Richard Wagner was born in Leipzig in 1813 and grew up in a theatrical family in Dresden and Leipzig. After years of struggle as a conductor in provincial theatres and a period of poverty in Paris, he had his first great success in Dresden with Rienzi in 1842 and became Kapellmeister there, following it with Der fliegende Holländer, Tannhäuser and Lohengrin. His part in the Dresden uprising of 1849 forced him into exile in Switzerland, where he wrote the theoretical writings that shaped his later work and began Der Ring des Nibelungen. In 1864 the young King Ludwig II of Bavaria rescued him from debt and became his patron. He married Cosima von Bülow, Liszt's daughter, in 1870, and built the Festspielhaus in Bayreuth, where the Ring was first performed complete in 1876. His last work, Parsifal, appeared there in 1882. He died in Venice in 1883.

Wagner's music dramas abandon the division into arias and recitative for a continuous flow of music, woven from leitmotifs: short themes associated with characters, objects and ideas, transformed as the drama unfolds. His chromatic harmony, especially in Tristan und Isolde, pushed tonality to new limits, and his huge orchestra created new sonorities. Few artists have been as influential or as divisive. His writings include virulent antisemitism, notably Das Judenthum in der Musik, and his works were later exploited by the Nazis, which continues to shadow his legacy.

name: Giuseppe Verdi
birthplace: Le Roncole, near Busseto, Duchy of Parma
bio: The greatest Italian opera composer of the nineteenth century, Verdi wrote Rigoletto, La traviata, Aida and Otello, and became a symbol of Italian unity.
bio_full: Giuseppe Verdi was born in 1813 in the village of Le Roncole near Busseto, the son of an innkeeper. A local merchant, Antonio Barezzi, supported his studies; he was rejected by the Milan Conservatory but studied privately and married Barezzi's daughter Margherita. The deaths of his two children and wife in 1838–40 devastated him, but Nabucco at La Scala in 1842 made him famous. Through what he called his years in the galley he wrote opera after opera, culminating in Rigoletto, Il trovatore and La traviata (1851–53). Later works included Don Carlos for Paris and Aida for Cairo (1871). He became a national figure during the Risorgimento, briefly served in Italy's first parliament and farmed his estate at Sant'Agata with his second wife, the soprano Giuseppina Strepponi. In old age, with the librettist Arrigo Boito, he produced Otello and Falstaff. He died in Milan in 1901.

Verdi's operas centre on intense human conflicts, between fathers and daughters, love and duty, the individual and power, conveyed through memorable melody and strong theatrical pacing. Over his long career he loosened the conventional number structure of Italian opera into more continuous drama, while keeping the primacy of the voice. His Requiem of 1874 is one of the great choral works. Verdi's operas remain the core of the international repertory.

name: Johannes Brahms
bio: Brahms united Romantic feeling with the forms and counterpoint of Bach and Beethoven in symphonies, concertos, chamber music and A German Requiem.
bio_full: Johannes Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833, the son of a double bass player, and earned money as a boy playing piano in dockside taverns. In 1853, touring with the violinist Ede Reményi, he met Joseph Joachim and then Robert and Clara Schumann; Robert proclaimed him the coming genius in a famous article. After Robert's breakdown Brahms helped Clara, and they remained deeply close for life. He settled in Vienna in 1863, where A German Requiem (1868) and the Hungarian Dances brought him fame and financial security. He took more than twenty years to complete his First Symphony (1876), conscious of Beethoven's shadow, then wrote three more in less than a decade. He never married and died in Vienna in 1897.

Brahms was a conservative in form and a master of variation, counterpoint and developing small motifs, yet his music is warm, autumnal and often passionate. He studied early music deeply and edited works by Couperin and others. Critics such as Eduard Hanslick set him up as the opposite of Wagner and Liszt, in what became known as the War of the Romantics. Schoenberg later wrote an essay called Brahms the Progressive, arguing that his methods pointed to modern music.

name: Georges Bizet
bio: Bizet's Carmen, a failure at its 1875 premiere, became one of the most popular operas ever written.
bio_full: Georges Bizet was born in Paris in 1838 into a musical family and entered the Paris Conservatoire before his tenth birthday. A brilliant pianist, he wrote the Symphony in C at seventeen and won the Prix de Rome in 1857. Back in Paris he struggled to establish himself in the theatre, producing Les pêcheurs de perles (1863) and La jolie fille de Perth, and earning a living from arrangements and teaching. In 1872 his incidental music for Daudet's play L'Arlésienne showed his maturity. Carmen opened at the Opéra-Comique in March 1875 to a mixed and partly scandalised reception. Bizet died of a heart attack three months later, aged thirty-six.

Bizet's music is marked by vivid melody, clear orchestration and dramatic directness. Carmen broke the conventions of the family-oriented Opéra-Comique with its working-class characters, sensuality and on-stage murder. Its Spanish colour draws on popular songs, and its realism anticipated Italian verismo. Within a few years the opera was triumphing across Europe; Tchaikovsky predicted it would become the most popular opera in the world, and Nietzsche held it up against Wagner.

name: Bedřich Smetana
bio: The founder of Czech national music, Smetana wrote the opera The Bartered Bride and the cycle of symphonic poems Má vlast.
bio_full: Bedřich Smetana was born in Litomyšl in eastern Bohemia in 1824, the son of a brewer, and grew up speaking German, as did most educated Czechs then. He studied in Prague, opened a music school there with Liszt's encouragement, and took part in the revolution of 1848. From 1856 to 1861 he worked in Gothenburg in Sweden. Returning to Prague as Czech national feeling rose, he wrote operas for the new Provisional Theatre, including The Bartered Bride (1866), and became its principal conductor. In 1874 he went completely deaf, probably as a result of syphilis, but went on to compose Má vlast and his autobiographical string quartet From My Life. He died in a Prague asylum in 1884.

Smetana drew on Czech dances such as the polka and furiant, on Czech history and legend and on the Bohemian landscape, while using the progressive techniques of Liszt and Wagner. His eight operas created a Czech national repertoire, and Má vlast, especially Vltava, which follows the river from its sources through Prague, became a symbol of the nation. The Prague Spring festival opens each year on the anniversary of his death with Má vlast.

name: Modest Mussorgsky
bio: The most original of the Russian 'Mighty Handful', Mussorgsky wrote the opera Boris Godunov and Pictures at an Exhibition in a raw, deeply Russian idiom.
bio_full: Modest Mussorgsky was born in 1839 on his family's estate at Karevo in the Pskov region and trained for the army, serving as an officer in the Preobrazhensky Guards. In the late 1850s he joined the circle of Mily Balakirev, later called the Mighty Handful, which also included Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov and aimed to create a national Russian music. After the emancipation of the serfs ruined his family's estate, he worked as a civil servant. Boris Godunov, rejected in its first version, was staged at the Mariinsky Theatre in 1874. Alcoholism wrecked his health, and he died in a military hospital in Saint Petersburg in 1881, leaving several works unfinished.

Mussorgsky sought to capture the rhythms of Russian speech and the life of the people with brutal honesty, using modal harmonies, folk-like melody and unconventional forms that his peers considered crude. After his death Rimsky-Korsakov revised and reorchestrated Boris and other works, which helped them win fame but smoothed away their roughness; today the original versions are preferred. Debussy, Ravel and later Shostakovich admired him greatly, and Ravel's orchestration of Pictures at an Exhibition is famous.

name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
bio: The most popular Russian composer, Tchaikovsky wrote the ballets Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker, six symphonies and the opera Eugene Onegin.
bio_full: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was born in 1840 in Votkinsk in the Urals, the son of a mining engineer. He trained at the School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg and worked as a civil servant before studying at the new Saint Petersburg Conservatory under Anton Rubinstein. From 1866 he taught at the Moscow Conservatory. His disastrous marriage in 1877 to a former student, entered partly to hide his homosexuality, collapsed within weeks. For thirteen years he received an allowance from the wealthy widow Nadezhda von Meck, with whom he corresponded intensely but never met, which allowed him to devote himself to composition. He became internationally famous, conducting in Europe and opening Carnegie Hall in New York in 1891. He died in Saint Petersburg in 1893, nine days after conducting the premiere of his Sixth Symphony; the official cause was cholera, though other theories have circulated and are disputed.

Tchaikovsky combined Russian melody with Western training in counterpoint and form. His music is direct and emotionally open, rich in long melodies, brilliant orchestration and dance rhythms. His ballets, created for the Imperial Theatres, raised ballet music to symphonic stature. Though members of the Mighty Handful thought him too Westernised, he is now seen as a quintessentially Russian voice, and works such as the First Piano Concerto, the Violin Concerto and the Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Symphonies remain cornerstones of the repertoire.

name: Antonín Dvořák
bio: Dvořák brought Czech folk spirit into symphonies, concertos and chamber music, and in America wrote the New World Symphony.
bio_full: Antonín Dvořák was born in 1841 in Nelahozeves near Prague, the son of a butcher and innkeeper, and trained at the Prague organ school. For years he played viola in the orchestra of the Provisional Theatre, under Smetana among others. An Austrian state stipend brought him to the attention of Brahms, who recommended him to his publisher Simrock, and the Slavonic Dances of 1878 made him famous. He was especially popular in England, where he visited nine times. From 1892 to 1895 he directed the National Conservatory of Music in New York, writing the New World Symphony, the American String Quartet and the Cello Concerto. Back in Prague he taught at the conservatory, became its director and wrote operas, including Rusalka. He died in Prague in 1904.

Dvořák's music combines Classical forms, learned partly from Brahms, with Czech and Slavonic dance rhythms and melodies, though he usually invented his own folk-like themes. In America he urged composers to build a national music on African American spirituals and Native American music, which he believed held the seeds of a new style. His nine symphonies, the Cello Concerto, the Dumky Trio and Rusalka are mainstays of the repertory.

name: Edvard Grieg
bio: Norway's leading composer, Grieg wrote the Piano Concerto in A minor, the music for Ibsen's Peer Gynt and many lyric piano pieces and songs.
bio_full: Edvard Grieg was born in Bergen in 1843 into a merchant family. On the advice of the violinist Ole Bull he studied at the Leipzig Conservatory. In Copenhagen he met the young Norwegian nationalist composer Rikard Nordraak, who inspired him to seek a Norwegian voice. He married his cousin, the soprano Nina Hagerup, who sang many of his songs. His Piano Concerto (1868) won the praise of Liszt, and Ibsen invited him to write music for Peer Gynt, first staged in 1876. A state pension from 1874 let him concentrate on composing. From 1885 he lived at Troldhaugen near Bergen, touring Europe as conductor and pianist, and he died in Bergen in 1907.

Grieg drew on Norwegian folk music, its dance rhythms, drones and modal colour, and was at his best in short forms: ten books of Lyric Pieces for piano and around 180 songs. His fresh harmonies influenced Debussy and Ravel. Pieces such as Morning Mood and In the Hall of the Mountain King became among the most familiar in all classical music.

name: Anton Bruckner
bio: An organist and devout Catholic, Bruckner wrote vast, cathedral-like symphonies that fuse Wagnerian harmony with the tradition of Beethoven and Schubert.
bio_full: Anton Bruckner was born in 1824 in Ansfelden in Upper Austria, the son of a village schoolmaster. He became a choirboy and later organist at the monastery of St Florian, and in 1855 cathedral organist in Linz, while studying counterpoint by correspondence with the theorist Simon Sechter well into his late thirties. A performance of Tannhäuser in 1863 overwhelmed him, and Wagner became his idol. From 1868 he lived in Vienna, teaching at the conservatory and university and famous as an organ improviser. His symphonies met hostility from critics such as Hanslick, who saw him as a Wagnerian, but the Seventh Symphony (1884) brought success. He died in Vienna in 1896, leaving his Ninth Symphony unfinished, and is buried beneath the organ at St Florian.

Bruckner's eleven symphonies, including two early ones, unfold on a huge scale through blocks of sound, sudden silences, long crescendos and brass chorales that recall the organ and church music. He revised them repeatedly, often at the urging of friends, so that several survive in multiple versions, a problem that still occupies editors and conductors. His masses and motets are also central to Catholic choral music.

name: Giacomo Puccini
bio: Heir to Verdi, Puccini wrote La bohème, Tosca and Madama Butterfly, among the most performed operas in the world.
bio_full: Giacomo Puccini was born in Lucca in 1858 into a family that had provided the town's church musicians for four generations. A performance of Verdi's Aida in Pisa decided him on opera, and he studied at the Milan Conservatory with Amilcare Ponchielli. The publisher Giulio Ricordi supported him from his first opera, and Manon Lescaut (1893) made his name. La bohème (1896), Tosca (1900) and Madama Butterfly (1904) followed, the last a failure at its premiere before revision made it a triumph. He lived mostly at Torre del Lago, by a lake in Tuscany, where he loved hunting. La fanciulla del West premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in New York in 1910. He died in Brussels in 1924 during treatment for throat cancer, leaving Turandot unfinished; Franco Alfano completed it.

Puccini had an unmatched gift for soaring, emotional melody and a sure sense of theatre, building scenes with cinematic pacing and orchestral detail. Associated with the verismo movement's realism, he favoured intimate dramas of love and suffering, especially of young women. He absorbed contemporary harmony, including Debussy's, and used exotic colour in Butterfly and Turandot. Critics long patronised his popularity, but his craft is now widely admired.

name: Gustav Mahler
bio: Conductor and composer, Mahler wrote ten vast symphonies and orchestral song cycles that, in his words, embraced the whole world.
bio_full: Gustav Mahler was born in 1860 in Kaliště in Bohemia into a German-speaking Jewish family and grew up in Jihlava. He studied at the Vienna Conservatory and rose through opera houses from Ljubljana and Olomouc to Kassel, Prague, Leipzig, Budapest and Hamburg. In 1897, having converted to Catholicism, partly because Jews were barred from the post, he became director of the Vienna Court Opera, which he transformed through ten demanding years. He composed mainly in summer holidays in his lakeside composing huts. In 1902 he married Alma Schindler. In 1907 his elder daughter died and he was diagnosed with a heart condition, and he left Vienna to conduct at the Metropolitan Opera and the New York Philharmonic. He died in Vienna in 1911, leaving his Tenth Symphony unfinished.

Mahler's symphonies combine the sublime and the banal: folk songs, marches, Ländler, birdcalls and hymns sit beside vast climaxes and music of profound spiritual searching. Several include voices, and his song cycles, such as Kindertotenlieder and Das Lied von der Erde, are closely tied to them. He expanded the orchestra and the length of the symphony. Long neglected after his death and banned by the Nazis, his music was championed by Bruno Walter and Leonard Bernstein and became central to the repertoire from the 1960s.

name: Claude Debussy
bio: Debussy freed harmony from traditional rules and created a new music of colour and atmosphere, from Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune to La mer.
bio_full: Claude Debussy was born in 1862 in Saint-Germain-en-Laye near Paris. He entered the Paris Conservatoire at ten, was a rebellious student of harmony, and in 1880–82 spent summers as house pianist to Tchaikovsky's patron Nadezhda von Meck. He won the Prix de Rome in 1884. At the 1889 Paris Exposition he heard a Javanese gamelan, which deeply influenced him. He moved in Symbolist literary circles and set poems by Baudelaire, Verlaine and Mallarmé, whose poem inspired Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894). His only completed opera, Pelléas et Mélisande, premiered in 1902. His private life caused scandal when he left his first wife for Emma Bardac. He died of cancer in Paris in 1918 during the German bombardment.

Debussy disliked the label Impressionism but sought in music something like the suggestion and nuance of the Symbolist poets and Impressionist painters. He used whole-tone and pentatonic scales, medieval modes, parallel chords and unresolved dissonance for their colour rather than their function, and preferred fluid forms to developmental argument. His Préludes and Images for piano, La mer and Jeux changed the course of twentieth-century music, influencing composers from Ravel and Stravinsky to Messiaen, Boulez and jazz musicians.

name: Richard Strauss
bio: Strauss wrote brilliant tone poems such as Also sprach Zarathustra and operas from the shocking Salome to the nostalgic Der Rosenkavalier.
bio_full: Richard Strauss was born in Munich in 1864, the son of Franz Strauss, principal horn player of the court orchestra. He was a prolific prodigy, and the conductor Hans von Bülow gave him his first posts. Tone poems such as Don Juan (1889), Till Eulenspiegels lustige Streiche and Also sprach Zarathustra made him the leading German composer after Wagner, while he also built a major career as a conductor in Weimar, Munich, Berlin and Vienna. With the poet Hugo von Hofmannsthal he wrote Elektra, Der Rosenkavalier and Ariadne auf Naxos. In 1933 he accepted the presidency of the Nazi Reich Music Chamber, resigning in 1935 after a letter to his Jewish librettist Stefan Zweig was intercepted; his conduct under the regime is still debated. He died in Garmisch in 1949, a year after writing the Four Last Songs.

Strauss's tone poems display virtuoso orchestration and vivid, sometimes humorous storytelling. Salome and Elektra pushed harmony towards dissonance and expressionism, but with Der Rosenkavalier he turned towards a lush, Mozartian lyricism and waltz-filled nostalgia, which he kept for the rest of his life. His writing for the soprano voice, from the Marschallin to the Four Last Songs, is especially cherished.

name: Jean Sibelius
bio: Finland's national composer, Sibelius wrote Finlandia and seven symphonies of remarkable concentration and organic growth.
bio_full: Jean Sibelius was born in 1865 in Hämeenlinna in the Grand Duchy of Finland, then part of the Russian empire, into a Swedish-speaking family. He studied in Helsinki, Berlin and Vienna, and returned home to write works inspired by the Finnish epic Kalevala, beginning with Kullervo (1892). As Russian pressure on Finland increased, works such as Finlandia (1899) became symbols of national resistance, and from 1897 a state pension supported him. In 1904 he moved to Ainola, a house in the forests at Järvenpää. After the Seventh Symphony (1924) and the tone poem Tapiola (1926) he published almost nothing, apparently destroying an Eighth Symphony, and lived three decades of silence before dying in 1957.

Sibelius's symphonies develop themes from small cells into large, organic wholes, with long pedal points, brooding orchestral textures and climaxes evoking the Nordic landscape. He spoke of the profound logic that connects the motifs. Very popular in Britain and the United States in the 1930s, he was later dismissed by modernists, but his treatment of slowly changing textures has influenced composers from spectralists to minimalists.

name: Erik Satie
bio: An eccentric of Montmartre, Satie wrote deliberately simple, ironic pieces such as the Gymnopédies and influenced generations of experimental composers.
bio_full: Erik Satie was born in Honfleur in 1866 and studied without distinction at the Paris Conservatoire. In Montmartre he played piano at the cabaret Le Chat Noir, joined a Rosicrucian sect and founded his own church with himself as its only member. The Gymnopédies (1888) and Gnossiennes belong to these years. In 1898 he moved to the suburb of Arcueil, walking to Paris each day. At nearly forty he enrolled at the Schola Cantorum to study counterpoint. Championed by Ravel and Cocteau, he wrote the ballet Parade (1917) with Picasso's designs for the Ballets Russes, and became a guiding spirit of the younger composers known as Les Six. He died in Paris in 1925.

Satie rejected the grandeur of Wagner and the refinement of Debussy alike, favouring bare textures, repetition and static harmony, often with absurd titles and performance instructions. His idea of furniture music, meant to be heard but not listened to, anticipated ambient music. John Cage championed him, staging his Vexations, a short piece marked to be repeated 840 times.

name: Maurice Ravel
bio: A master of orchestration and precise craftsmanship, Ravel wrote Boléro, Daphnis et Chloé and some of the finest piano music of the century.
bio_full: Maurice Ravel was born in 1875 in Ciboure in the French Basque country, to a Swiss engineer father and a Basque mother, and grew up in Paris. He studied at the Conservatoire, where Gabriel Fauré taught him composition. His repeated failures to win the Prix de Rome culminated in a scandal in 1905 that led to the director's resignation. Works such as Jeux d'eau, the String Quartet and Miroirs established him alongside Debussy. For Diaghilev's Ballets Russes he wrote Daphnis et Chloé (1912). He served as a driver at the front in the First World War, and Le tombeau de Couperin commemorates friends killed in it. He toured North America in 1928, and Boléro appeared that year. A neurological illness ended his composing in the early 1930s, and he died in Paris in 1937 after brain surgery.

Ravel admired clarity, craftsmanship and objectivity, describing himself as artificial by nature. He was drawn to Classical forms, dance, Spanish music, fairy tales and jazz, as in his two piano concertos and Violin Sonata. His orchestration, including his arrangement of Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition, is a model of brilliance and precision. He is often grouped with Debussy as an Impressionist, but his music is more sharply drawn and Classical in its proportions.

name: Arnold Schoenberg
bio: Schoenberg led music beyond tonality and created the twelve-tone method, one of the most influential developments of twentieth-century music.
bio_full: Arnold Schoenberg was born in Vienna in 1874 into a Jewish family and was largely self-taught, apart from lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky, whose sister he married. His early works, such as the string sextet Verklärte Nacht (1899) and Gurre-Lieder, extend Wagner and Brahms. From around 1908 he abandoned key altogether in works such as the Five Orchestral Pieces, Erwartung and Pierrot lunaire. He was also an Expressionist painter linked with Kandinsky's Blue Rider group. His teaching drew pupils including Berg and Webern. In the early 1920s he formulated the method of composing with twelve tones. He taught at the Prussian Academy of Arts in Berlin until the Nazis dismissed him in 1933; he formally returned to Judaism in Paris and emigrated to the United States, teaching at the University of California, Los Angeles. He died in Los Angeles in 1951, leaving his opera Moses und Aron unfinished.

Schoenberg saw his work as the logical continuation of the German tradition, from Bach and Brahms to Wagner and Mahler. He called his abandonment of tonality the emancipation of dissonance. The twelve-tone method arranges the twelve notes into a fixed series, which can be inverted, reversed and transposed to generate a whole work. Few composers have been as controversial: his music has never been popular, but its ideas dominated composition for decades after the Second World War, and his textbooks on harmony and composition are still widely read.

name: Igor Stravinsky
bio: Stravinsky's ballets for the Ballets Russes, above all The Rite of Spring, revolutionised rhythm, and he went on to lead neoclassicism and later to adopt serialism.
bio_full: Igor Stravinsky was born in 1882 at Oranienbaum near Saint Petersburg, the son of a leading bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. He studied law but took private lessons in composition with Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. Sergei Diaghilev commissioned The Firebird for his Ballets Russes in Paris in 1910, followed by Petrushka (1911) and The Rite of Spring (1913), whose premiere caused one of the most famous scandals in music history. Cut off from Russia by war and revolution, he lived in Switzerland and then France, becoming a French citizen in 1934. In 1939 he moved to the United States, settling in Hollywood, and became an American citizen in 1945. From the late 1940s his assistant Robert Craft helped turn him towards serial music. He died in New York in 1971 and was buried in Venice near Diaghilev.

Stravinsky's Russian ballets use folk-derived melodies, layered ostinatos, clashing harmonies and violently shifting irregular metres. From Pulcinella (1920), based on eighteenth-century music, he led the neoclassical movement, borrowing older forms and styles with ironic detachment, as in the Symphony of Psalms and the opera The Rake's Progress. His late serial works, such as Agon and Threni, completed a career of constant reinvention. Few composers had a wider influence on the music of the twentieth century.

name: Béla Bartók
bio: Composer, pianist and pioneering folk-music collector, Bartók forged a modern style from Eastern European peasant music.
bio_full: Béla Bartók was born in 1881 in Nagyszentmiklós, then in Hungary and now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. He studied piano and composition at the Budapest Academy of Music, where he later taught piano for nearly three decades. From 1905, with his friend Zoltán Kodály, he travelled through villages in Hungary, Slovakia, Romania and as far as North Africa and Turkey, recording thousands of peasant songs on wax cylinders and transcribing them in meticulous detail. His opera Bluebeard's Castle and the ballet The Miraculous Mandarin date from the 1910s. Opposed to the Nazis and to Hungary's alliance with Germany, he emigrated to the United States in 1940, where he lived in poor health and financial difficulty. The Concerto for Orchestra, commissioned by Serge Koussevitzky, was a success in 1944. He died of leukaemia in New York in 1945.

Bartók distinguished real peasant music from the urban gypsy style that Liszt and Brahms had used as 'Hungarian'. He absorbed its modes, irregular rhythms and ornaments into a style of great energy and rigour, using dissonance, symmetry and night music evoking nocturnal nature sounds. His six string quartets are among the most important since Beethoven's. His teaching pieces, the six books of Mikrokosmos, trace a path from simple exercises to concert works, and his ethnomusicological work remains a model.

name: Alban Berg
bio: Schoenberg's pupil Berg combined atonality and twelve-tone technique with Romantic expressiveness, above all in the opera Wozzeck.
bio_full: Alban Berg was born in Vienna in 1885 into a prosperous family. Largely self-taught, he began studying with Schoenberg in 1904 and remained his devoted friend. He served in the Austrian army during the First World War, an experience that shaped Wozzeck, the opera based on Büchner's fragmentary play, which premiered in Berlin in 1925 and made him famous. He lived quietly in Vienna, adopting the twelve-tone method in the Lyric Suite for string quartet (1926), which modern research has shown contains a secret programme about his love for Hanna Fuchs-Robettin. Under the Nazis his music was branded degenerate. He died in Vienna on Christmas Eve 1935 from an infected insect sting, leaving his second opera, Lulu, incomplete.

Berg's music is the most lyrical and approachable of the Second Viennese School. He used strict forms in unexpected ways (each scene of Wozzeck is built on a traditional form such as a passacaglia or suite) and often worked hidden numbers and ciphers into his scores. His twelve-tone rows often contain tonal triads, allowing reminiscences of tonality, as in the quotation of a Bach chorale in the Violin Concerto. Wozzeck is one of the most performed operas of the century.

name: Anton Webern
bio: Webern's brief, crystalline works pushed Schoenberg's methods to radical concentration and became a model for the post-war avant-garde.
bio_full: Anton Webern was born in Vienna in 1883 into an aristocratic family, which dropped the 'von' after titles were abolished in 1918. He studied musicology at the University of Vienna, writing a doctorate on the Renaissance composer Heinrich Isaac, and from 1904 studied composition with Schoenberg. He worked as a theatre conductor and later as conductor of the Vienna Workers' Symphony Concerts, but the Nazis banned his music, and in the war years he lived mainly by proof-reading and teaching. In September 1945, shortly after the war ended, he stepped outside a house in Mittersill to smoke a cigar during a curfew and was shot dead by an American army cook.

Webern's complete numbered works can be heard in a few hours. His pieces are tiny in scale, with single notes passed between instruments in a technique called pointillism, transparent textures and extreme dynamics, and after 1924 they use twelve-tone rows of great symmetry and canons inspired by his Renaissance studies. After the war Boulez, Stockhausen and others made him their model, and even Stravinsky praised him late in life.

name: Sergei Prokofiev
bio: Prokofiev combined steely modernism with lyrical melody in ballets such as Romeo and Juliet, the Classical Symphony and Peter and the Wolf.
bio_full: Sergei Prokofiev was born in 1891 at Sontsovka, an estate in what is now eastern Ukraine, where his father was manager. A prodigy, he entered the Saint Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen and shocked his teachers with his percussive, dissonant piano works. After the Revolution he left Russia in 1918, living in the United States, Germany and above all Paris, where he worked with Diaghilev. In 1936 he returned to the Soviet Union for good, writing Romeo and Juliet, Peter and the Wolf and the film score for Eisenstein's Alexander Nevsky. In 1948 he was denounced, with Shostakovich, for formalism, and his first wife Lina was sent to a labour camp. In poor health, he died in Moscow on 5 March 1953, the same day as Stalin, so his death went largely unnoticed.

Prokofiev's music combines motoric rhythms, sharp dissonance and sardonic wit with soaring lyrical melodies and traditional forms. His seven symphonies, five piano concertos, nine piano sonatas and the operas The Love for Three Oranges and War and Peace show his range. His later Soviet works are simpler in style, a shift both he and critics have explained partly by political pressure and partly by his own artistic development.

name: George Gershwin
bio: A Broadway and Tin Pan Alley songwriter who brought jazz into the concert hall, Gershwin wrote Rhapsody in Blue and the opera Porgy and Bess.
bio_full: George Gershwin was born in Brooklyn in 1898 to Russian Jewish immigrant parents. He left school at fifteen to work as a song plugger on Tin Pan Alley, and his song Swanee, recorded by Al Jolson in 1920, made him rich. With his brother Ira as lyricist he wrote a series of Broadway musicals, including Lady, Be Good and Of Thee I Sing, and standards such as The Man I Love and I Got Rhythm. Paul Whiteman's commission of Rhapsody in Blue (1924) launched his concert career, followed by the Piano Concerto in F and An American in Paris. Porgy and Bess (1935) was his most ambitious work. He moved to Hollywood to write film songs and died there of a brain tumour in 1937, aged thirty-eight.

Gershwin's music fuses the melody and harmony of popular song, the blue notes and syncopation of jazz and the forms of classical music. Ravel and Schoenberg admired him. Porgy and Bess, written for an African American cast, was long controversial for its portrayal of Black life by white creators, but songs such as Summertime became jazz standards and the opera is now staged by major companies worldwide.

name: Louis Armstrong
bio: Trumpeter and singer, Armstrong turned jazz into a soloist's art, and his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings are founding classics of the music.
bio_full: Louis Armstrong was born in 1901 in a poor district of New Orleans. Sent to the Colored Waifs' Home for Boys after firing a pistol on New Year's Eve, he learned the cornet in its band. He played on riverboats and in New Orleans clubs, mentored by King Oliver, whom he joined in Chicago in 1922. After a spell with Fletcher Henderson's orchestra in New York, he recorded with his Hot Five and Hot Seven bands in Chicago from 1925 to 1928, among the most influential records in jazz. In the 1930s he became a big-band star and film actor, and from 1947 he toured the world with his All Stars, becoming known as Ambassador Satch. His recordings of Hello, Dolly! and What a Wonderful World were huge popular hits. He died in New York in 1971.

Armstrong's improvisations showed that a jazz solo could tell a coherent, dramatic story, and his swinging rhythm transformed how jazz was played. His warm, gravelly voice and scat singing shaped popular singing, influencing figures from Bing Crosby to Billie Holiday. Some later musicians criticised his genial stage persona, but he spoke out against segregation, notably during the Little Rock school crisis of 1957.

name: Duke Ellington
bio: Bandleader, pianist and composer, Ellington made the jazz orchestra a medium for composition, writing hundreds of pieces for his band over fifty years.
bio_full: Edward Kennedy Ellington was born in Washington, D.C., in 1899 to a middle-class family; his elegant manners earned him the nickname Duke. He moved to New York in 1923 and from 1927 to 1931 led the house band at the Cotton Club in Harlem, whose radio broadcasts made him nationally famous. He kept his orchestra together continuously for nearly half a century, touring the world, and with his collaborator Billy Strayhorn wrote suites, film scores and sacred concerts. His 1956 appearance at the Newport Jazz Festival revived his career. He died in New York in 1974.

Ellington composed with the particular sound of each player in mind, such as the growling trumpet of Bubber Miley or the sweet alto saxophone of Johnny Hodges, creating textures and colours that no one else could reproduce. His works range from three-minute pieces such as Mood Indigo and Ko-Ko to extended suites like Black, Brown and Beige, a tone parallel to the history of African Americans. He disliked the label jazz and preferred to call his work American music. He is widely regarded as the greatest jazz composer.

name: Dmitri Shostakovich
bio: The leading Soviet composer, Shostakovich wrote fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets under the shadow of Stalinist censorship.
bio_full: Dmitri Shostakovich was born in Saint Petersburg in 1906 and studied at the Petrograd Conservatory, where his First Symphony (1926) won international attention. His opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District was a success until January 1936, when an article in Pravda, reportedly after Stalin attended, condemned it as 'muddle instead of music'. Facing the danger of arrest, he withdrew his Fourth Symphony and in 1937 presented the Fifth, a public rehabilitation. His Seventh Symphony, partly written in besieged Leningrad, became a symbol of resistance. In 1948 he was denounced again for formalism and lost his teaching posts.
