After Stalin's death he gradually regained position, joining the Communist Party in 1960. He died in Moscow in 1975.

Shostakovich's music combines Mahlerian scale, biting irony, grotesque humour, banal marches and profound tragedy. Whether works such as the Fifth Symphony carry hidden dissent is much debated, especially since the disputed memoir Testimony, published in 1979. His fifteen string quartets, more private in tone, include the Eighth, often heard as autobiographical, and he frequently used his musical monogram DSCH (D, E flat, C, B). He is among the most performed composers of the twentieth century.

name: Aaron Copland
bio: Copland created an American concert style of open harmonies and folk-inflected melodies in works such as Appalachian Spring.
bio_full: Aaron Copland was born in Brooklyn in 1900 to Lithuanian Jewish immigrants. In 1921 he went to France and studied with Nadia Boulanger, the first of many Americans to do so. Back in New York he wrote jazz-influenced works and dissonant modernist pieces, and organised concerts of new American music. In the 1930s and 1940s he turned to a simpler, more accessible style in the ballets Billy the Kid, Rodeo and Appalachian Spring, which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1945, as well as Fanfare for the Common Man and film scores. In 1953, at the height of McCarthyism, he was questioned by a Senate committee about his left-wing sympathies. He taught for many years at the Tanglewood summer school and in later life composed little but conducted widely. He died in 1990.

Copland's music is marked by wide-spaced open chords, clear textures and spare melodies, sometimes based on cowboy songs or Shaker hymns, evoking American landscapes and ideals. He also adopted twelve-tone technique in later works such as Connotations. Through his books, teaching and advocacy he became the dean of American composers.

name: Benjamin Britten
bio: The leading British composer of the twentieth century, Britten revived English opera with Peter Grimes and wrote the War Requiem.
bio_full: Benjamin Britten was born in Lowestoft in 1913, the son of a dentist, and studied privately with Frank Bridge and then at the Royal College of Music. In the 1930s he wrote music for documentary films and collaborated with W. H. Auden. A pacifist, he went to America with his partner, the tenor Peter Pears, in 1939, returning in 1942 as a conscientious objector. Peter Grimes, premiered at Sadler's Wells in June 1945, launched a series of operas including Billy Budd, The Turn of the Screw and Death in Venice. In 1948 he and Pears founded the Aldeburgh Festival in Suffolk. The War Requiem was written for the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral in 1962. He was made a life peer shortly before his death in Aldeburgh in 1976.

Britten's music is tonal but distinctively modern, with brilliant writing for voice, a keen sense of drama and often a theme of innocence destroyed or the outsider persecuted by society. He drew on Purcell, Mahler and Balinese gamelan, and wrote widely for amateurs and children, as in Noye's Fludde and The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra.

name: Olivier Messiaen
bio: A devout Catholic organist, Messiaen built a unique language from birdsong, Indian rhythms and colourful harmony, and taught many of the post-war avant-garde.
bio_full: Olivier Messiaen was born in Avignon in 1908, the son of a literature teacher and the poet Cécile Sauvage, and entered the Paris Conservatoire at eleven. In 1931 he became organist of the church of La Trinité in Paris, a post he held for over sixty years. Captured as a French soldier in 1940, he wrote the Quartet for the End of Time in a German prisoner-of-war camp in Silesia, where it was first performed in January 1941. After his release he taught at the Conservatoire, where his pupils included Boulez, Stockhausen and Xenakis. He married the pianist Yvonne Loriod, for whom he wrote much piano music. He spent years transcribing birdsong across the world, and in his seventies wrote the opera Saint François d'Assise. He died in 1992.

Messiaen's music is an expression of Catholic faith, often ecstatic and celebratory. He devised his modes of limited transposition, used rhythms derived from ancient Greek metres and Indian talas, and experienced harmonies as colours, a form of synaesthesia. His experiment Mode de valeurs et d'intensités (1949) inspired the integral serialism of his students. Works such as the Turangalîla-Symphonie and Catalogue d'oiseaux are among the most original of the century.

name: John Cage
bio: Cage's chance operations, prepared piano and the silent piece 4′33″ transformed ideas of what music could be.
bio_full: John Cage was born in Los Angeles in 1912, the son of an inventor. He studied with Henry Cowell and with Schoenberg, who later said he was not a composer but an inventor of genius. In Seattle and then New York he wrote for percussion ensembles and invented the prepared piano, with objects placed between the strings. From the 1940s he was the partner and collaborator of the choreographer Merce Cunningham. Study of Zen Buddhism and the I Ching led him from 1951 to compose by chance operations, as in Music of Changes, and in 1952 to the silent piece 4′33″. He also wrote influential books, notably Silence (1961), was a noted mycologist, and remained a central figure of the American avant-garde until his death in New York in 1992.

Cage aimed to free sounds from the composer's intentions, letting them be themselves. His use of chance, indeterminacy, electronics and everyday sounds influenced Fluxus, performance art, minimalism and later experimental music. He remains among the most debated figures of twentieth-century art.

name: Karlheinz Stockhausen
bio: A pioneer of electronic music and serialism, Stockhausen led the post-war avant-garde with works such as Gesang der Jünglinge.
bio_full: Karlheinz Stockhausen was born in 1928 at Mödrath near Cologne. His mother was killed under the Nazi euthanasia programme and his father died in the war. He studied in Cologne, then with Messiaen in Paris, and from 1953 worked at the electronic music studio of West German Radio in Cologne, which he later directed. He taught at the Darmstadt summer courses, which became a centre of the avant-garde. From 1977 to 2003 he composed Licht, a cycle of seven operas named for the days of the week. He died at Kürten in 2007.

Stockhausen applied serial organisation to all aspects of sound, combined electronic and acoustic sources, explored the spatial placement of sound and wrote 'intuitive music' guided by texts. Works such as Gruppen for three orchestras and Kontakte influenced not only composers but also rock and electronic musicians, and his face appears on the cover of the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper album.

name: György Ligeti
bio: Ligeti invented a music of dense, shimmering sound clouds in Atmosphères and Lux Aeterna, later heard in Kubrick's 2001.
bio_full: György Ligeti was born in 1923 into a Hungarian Jewish family in Transylvania, Romania. His father and brother died in Nazi concentration camps, and he survived forced labour. He studied and taught at the Budapest Academy, but his modernist leanings were stifled by the Communist regime. After the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising in 1956 he fled to Vienna and then Cologne, where he worked in the electronic studio and encountered the avant-garde. Atmosphères (1961) made his name. He taught for many years in Hamburg and later wrote the opera Le Grand Macabre, the Piano Études and concertos. He died in Vienna in 2006.

Ligeti's micropolyphony weaves many lines into a dense texture in which individual voices are lost but the mass of sound slowly changes. Later he drew on African polyrhythms, mechanical patterns and fractal geometry. Stanley Kubrick used several of his works in 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), without permission at first, bringing his music to a huge audience.

name: Terry Riley
bio: Riley's In C (1964), built from 53 short repeated patterns, is often regarded as the first major minimalist composition.
bio_full: Terry Riley was born in 1935 in Colfax, California, and studied at San Francisco State University and the University of California, Berkeley. Associated with La Monte Young and the San Francisco Tape Music Center, he experimented with tape loops. In C was first performed in San Francisco in November 1964 with Steve Reich among the players. Riley's later works include A Rainbow in Curved Air (1969) and many works for the Kronos Quartet. From 1970 he studied North Indian raga singing with Pandit Pran Nath.

Riley's music uses repetition, gradual change, modal harmony and improvisation, drawing on jazz and Indian music. His use of keyboards and tape delay influenced rock musicians including The Who and Soft Machine.

name: Steve Reich
bio: A founder of minimalism, Reich builds music from repeating patterns that gradually shift out of phase, culminating in Music for 18 Musicians.
bio_full: Steve Reich was born in New York in 1936, studied philosophy at Cornell University and composition at the Juilliard School and Mills College, where he studied with Luciano Berio. In San Francisco in the mid-1960s he discovered phasing with tape loops in It's Gonna Rain, then transferred it to live performers in Piano Phase. In 1966 he founded his own ensemble, and in 1970 he studied drumming in Ghana. Music for 18 Musicians (1976) brought him a wide audience. Later works such as Different Trains (1988), about wartime train journeys and the Holocaust, use recorded speech; Double Sextet won the Pulitzer Prize in 2009.

Reich's music emphasises audible processes: listeners can hear how the music is built as it unfolds. He draws on African drumming, Balinese gamelan, Hebrew cantillation, jazz and the Western canon from Pérotin to Bach. He has influenced composers, rock and electronic musicians alike.

name: Philip Glass
bio: Glass's repetitive, additive music reached mass audiences through operas such as Einstein on the Beach and his film scores.
bio_full: Philip Glass was born in Baltimore in 1937 and studied at the University of Chicago and the Juilliard School, then with Nadia Boulanger in Paris, where he also worked with the Indian musician Ravi Shankar. Back in New York he formed the Philip Glass Ensemble in 1968 and, for years, supported himself as a plumber and taxi driver. Einstein on the Beach, created with the director Robert Wilson, premiered in 1976. Satyagraha (1980), about Gandhi, and Akhnaten (1984) completed a trilogy of 'portrait operas'. His film scores include Koyaanisqatsi (1982) and The Hours (2002).

Glass prefers to speak of 'music with repetitive structures' rather than minimalism. His music develops through additive and subtractive rhythmic processes over simple harmonies, with the amplified sound of his ensemble. His later works, including fourteen symphonies and many string quartets, are more conventional in form, and his collaborations span rock, dance and theatre.

name: Arvo Pärt
bio: Pärt's spare, bell-like tintinnabuli style, steeped in chant and Orthodox spirituality, made him one of the most performed living composers.
bio_full: Arvo Pärt was born in 1935 in Paide, Estonia, and studied at the Tallinn Conservatory, working as a sound engineer for Estonian radio. His early works used serial techniques and collage, which brought him into conflict with Soviet authorities, especially Credo (1968) with its religious text. After years of near silence spent studying Gregorian chant and Renaissance polyphony, he emerged in 1976 with Für Alina and the tintinnabuli style, followed by Fratres, Tabula rasa and Spiegel im Spiegel (all 1977). He emigrated with his family in 1980, settling in Berlin, and returned to Estonia in the 2000s.

Tintinnabuli combines a melodic voice moving stepwise with a voice outlining the notes of a triad, like bells. The music is slow, quiet and often sacred, drawing on Orthodox Christianity, which Pärt adopted. Recordings on the ECM label from 1984 brought him international fame.
